facts.claim: Active social media use is linked to greater online support (r = .34), wellbeing (r = .15), positive affect (r = .11), and symptoms of anxiety (r = .12).
facts.quote: between-person associations for active SMU and greater online support (r = .34), wellbeing (r = .15), positive affect (r = .11), and symptoms of anxiety (r = .12)

facts.claim: Passive social media use is linked to greater online support (r = .15).
facts.quote: passive SMU and greater online support (r = .15)

facts.claim: Limiting social media use to approximately 30 minutes per day may lead to significant improvement in well-being.
facts.quote: Our findings strongly suggest that limiting social media use to approximately 30 minutes per day may lead to significant improvement in well-being.

facts.claim: Problematic social media use is linked to moderate correlations with depression and loneliness.
facts.quote: The mean correlations of problematic SM use with life satisfaction and self-esteem are small, whereas those of problematic SM use with depression and loneliness are moderate.

rejected.claim: Social media addiction is linked to loneliness (summary r = 0. 21, 95% CI = 0. 13-0. 29, P < 0. 001).
Problematic social media use is linked to depression (r=0. 273, P<. 0. 001), anxiety (r=0. 348, P<. 0. 001), and stress (r=0. 313, P<. 0. 001).
rejected.quote: Our metaregression shows moderate but statistically significant correlations between problematic social media use and depression (r=0. 273, P<. 0. 001), anxiety (r=0. 348, P<. 0. 001), and stress (r=0. 313, P<. 0. 001).
rejected.reason: quote not found in the source

research.angle: While social media addiction and problematic use are linked to loneliness and depression, active use is linked to greater online support and wellbeing.
research.verdict: The evidence shows that while problematic and addictive social media use correlates with loneliness and distress, active engagement can be linked to positive outcomes like online support.
research.caveat: Most findings are correlational, with the exception of one experiment suggesting that limiting use may reduce loneliness.
